doc.title: Rossano Sportiello interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 2, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Substitutions, learning bebop from Barry Harris and the overlap of styles
summary: He began as a Dixieland pianist until Barry Harris, watched up close, made him understand bebop; he argues the jazz styles of the 1940s all coexisted.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Do you have a way of thinking about choosing chord substitutions?

Yeah. Well I use very common substitutions, like of course the tri-tone substitution that every musician knows quite well. But you know really I started basically as a Dixieland piano player. But then about 15 years ago I met Barry Harris, that is the greatest jazz pianist, in my opinion, alive today. And Barry made me understand bebop you know.

Because you know, sometimes to understand something you have to be lucky enough to meet someone that you can watch close by what he’s doing. Because there is a human way and a musical way that you can get only just by standing there. And all of a sudden I understood so many more things about music. And we are so used to reason with labels. You know? This is swing, that’s Dixieland, that’s New Orleans, that’s bebop. But if we think of, for example, the early 40s, all the jazz was happening at the same time. Because there was Armstrong in his prime, Fats Waller died I think in 1943 so Fats Waller was

still around, but Bud Powell and Thelonious Monk, they were starting. So everything was happening at the same time. So there wasn’t a distinction in time like we do today. This was the period that is a way to make it simpler but it does not reflect the reality. So there was Teddy Wilson and that kind of rhythm section playing with Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, that they were blowing the bebop stuff. But of course they say that Charlie Parker came from Lester Young. So sometimes I believe that the language evolves. Anytime I try to play, because I’m inspired by someone else, that’s evolution. Because in the very moment that that material comes through you, it’s going to come out different. You know. And that’s it. So Bud Powell said that Art Tatum had a very strong influence in his playing and Billy Kyle too. Billy Kyle and Art Tatum were part of what Bud Powell tried to do. But then of course it came, Bud Powell, his own thing.
